newsitem.title: USA: U.S West spot power lower as temperatures rise.
newsitem.headline: U.S West spot power lower as temperatures rise.

text.p: Spot power prices in the U.S. West continued to fall amid moderate temperatures in most of the region as well as abundant hydropower supplies, market sources said Monday.
"People have realized winter has come and gone - it's 50 degrees (F) in Salt Lake City," said one trader.
He and others also emphasized that the Pacific Northwest has seen above-normal rain and snowfall so far this winter, making hydroelectric supplies plentiful.
"There is no load and a lot of water out there with nowhere to go," said the trader.

Bonneville Power Administration (BPA), the federal agency which markets the bulk of hydropower generated in the Northwest, continues to refrain from offering pre-scheduled power during peak demand hours, but market sources say the agency is selling in the real-time market.
"I think they have some flood-control issues," said a California utility trader.

A source at the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, which operates most of the federal dams in the Northwest, said despite the healthy water supply, there was no extra spill at hydropower projects over the weekend.
"Weekend loads are typically low, but BPA has successfully been able to market (the excess power)," he noted.
Firm, peak California-Oregon border (COB) electricity for Tuesday was assessed at $24.00-25.00 per megawatt hour (MWH), down from $28.00-29.00 for Monday.
Firm, off-peak COB power for Tuesday was also lower at $15.00-16.00.
Monday firm, peak power at Mid-Columbia (Mid-C) was down at $21.00-22.00, while off-peak was lower at Mid-C was also lower at $14.00-15.00.
Firm, peak Palo Verde (PV) electricity for Tuesday was quoted $22.00-23.00 per MWh, down from $26.00-28.00. Firm, off-peak PV power was lower at $13.00-14.00.
Tuesday firm, peak prices at Four Corners were quoted lower at $23.00-24.00 per MWh, while firm off-peak was assessed at $14.00-16.00.
